Lessons.Title: Equivalent Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Original warm-up Choral Count One-halves: count from 1/2 to8/2 in FOUR rows of TWO entries: 1/2,2/2;3/2,4/2;5/2,6/2;7/2,8/2. Compare the original previous lesson's four rows of four one-fourths ending 16/4. The source asks students to explain why 2/2 and4/4 name one.

Original Activity1 Equivalent to 1/2 uses six shaded squares A through F. Direct inspection of original six geometric SVGs confirms: A two of four equal parts shaded = HALF; B three of four equal parts shaded = NOT half; C one of two equal parts = HALF; D two of four equal horizontal bands = HALF; E one of two equal vertical halves = HALF; F one of two UNEQUAL horizontal parts, with a quarter area shaded = NOT half. Source-correct choices are A, C, D and E.

The distinction between D and F cannot be certified from counts or labels alone: D's four equal-width horizontal bands have two bands shaded, while F's two unequal parts leave only a quarter-sized colored region. Only equal AREA matters, and an explanation of why a diagram is or is not a half is teacher reviewed.

Activity2 source students physically use earlier fraction strips to find as MANY fractions equivalent to 1/2, 2/3, 6/6 and 3/4 as possible, rather than four single preset expected answers. Consistent-whole examples using the original fraction-strip families are: 1/2=2/4=3/6=4/8; 2/3=4/6; 6/6=2/2=3/3=4/4=8/8=1; 3/4=6/8. These are valid first-party oracles but DO NOT exhaust possible student-generated equivalences.

The original source teacher emphasizes equal length on strips and equal area in diagrams as the criterion for fraction equivalence. Students work together to compare their representations; a symbolic equality alone does not certify actual physical strip alignment or consistent definition of the whole.

Lesson synthesis encourages a number/area/length explanation of fraction equivalence, including 1/2=3/6. Original publisher Cool-down Find the Equivalent Fractions is teacher-gated and was not inspected or reproduced. The original standalone Student Task Statements PDF and Stage D tests remain unverified; all new displayed drawings are independent first-party educational models.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fractions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fractions of one consistent whole that have the same value, area or length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiplying both top and bottom by the same positive integer preserves fraction value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal-sized parts
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction of a shape must be made of equal-area pieces; arbitrary drawn regions do not create halves.
KeyConcepts.Rule: One of two unequal pieces does not necessarily equal 1/2.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original F shades one-quarter of a square although it has two regions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction-strip comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal-length strips represent the same fraction size when referred to the same original unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare physical marked lengths of the same whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original A–F shaded figures
WorkedExamples.Question: Which original shapes shade exactly a half of the whole?
WorkedExamples.Method: Assess area geometry, not number of separate regions.
Steps: A:2/4 shaded equal areas = half; B:3/4 = not half.
C:1/2 = half; D:2/4 equal areas = half.
E:1/2 = half; F:1 of 2 UNEQUAL areas, shaded quarter only = not half.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source six original SVG files directly inspected.

WorkedExamples.Title: One half as fourths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find fourths that cover one half of the same whole.
WorkedExamples.Method: Partition into four congruent parts and count two.
Steps: Divide a whole into four equal areas.

WorkedExamples.Title: One half as sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Make half with sixth-sized strip pieces.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use same whole and count three of six.
Steps: Six equal segments divide one full strip.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two thirds and sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find a sixths fraction equivalent to 2/3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Split each third into two equal pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Six sixths and full wholes
WorkedExamples.Question: What other fraction strips have the value 6/6?
WorkedExamples.Method: All parts shaded in a whole.
Steps: Six sixths make one complete unit.
Check all strips are one same-whole length.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three fourths and eighths
WorkedExamples.Question: What eighths equal 3/4?
WorkedExamples.Method: Split each fourth into two eighths.
Steps: Three quarter segments become six eighth segments.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mark original F as 1/2 because two parts are shown.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: F's regions are unequal, one colored region equals only 1/4 of entire square.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify equal area before naming fraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mark B as 1/2 because a majority shaded.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: B shades 3/4, not two equal quarters.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare shaded fraction with exactly one half.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Give just one accepted answer for each of the four strip prompts.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity asks pupils to find as many valid equivalences as they can.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept all correctly explained same-whole lengths.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up from 1/2 through8/2 in four rows of two, compared to the earlier one-fourths count.
Original A,C,D,E show half; B=3/4 and F=1/4 with UNEQUAL regions.
Source requires geometric same-whole evidence; protected Cool-down, student task PDF, tests and Stage D deferred.
